articles.headline: CoreWeave Stock Sinks as Investors Discover AI Clouds Come With Debt
articles.dek: The biggest neocloud has lost roughly two-thirds of its peak value, carries 15% yield debt, and awaits a rescue from its largest shareholder, who says none is needed.
articles.catch_up: CoreWeave rents out Nvidia chips to AI customers and has funded its data center buildout largely with borrowed money. Rising interest rates and doubts about AI spending have hit the whole neocloud sector this month.
articles.why_it_matters: If the companies building AI capacity cannot borrow at tolerable rates, the buildout slows, and so do the earnings forecasts that have supported much of the stock market. Investors in tech debt and AI-linked shares are being reminded that leverage works in both directions.
body: CoreWeave shares are down 35% this month, according to CNBC, after an 8% drop on Thursday, leaving the company valued at about $31 billion. That compares with a peak of roughly $90 billion three months after its March IPO last year. Its unsecured bonds now yield about 15%, which is the market's way of saying it would like to be paid generously for its optimism.

Translation: a yield is the annual return a bond buyer demands, and when it climbs, borrowing gets more expensive for the issuer. CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, trade at 1,115 basis points, or 11.15%. Translation: a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, and 1,115 of them is what insurers charge when they have read the balance sheet.

The pain is not confined to one company. CNBC reported that Nebius is down 32% this month and IREN is down 39%. Australia's NextDC fell 40% in a day after cutting its earnings forecast, and Firmus scrapped its IPO citing market volatility. Nscale, which filed to list in New York last month, now has to decide whether to proceed. Investing.com reported that short sellers, who profit when stocks fall, are sitting on about $6 billion in unrealized gains.

The backdrop is not friendly. The 10-year Treasury yield stood at 5.12% on October 20, and the 2-year at 4.79%. Barclays credit analyst Andrew Keches told clients sentiment is "decidedly negative," citing how fast "AI vibes" shift. It is a notable development when a bank analyst puts the word vibes in a research note about corporate credit.

CoreWeave's exposure is specific. More than two-thirds of last year's revenue came from Microsoft, and Nvidia owns about 9% of the company. It has about $20.7 billion of debt due through 2030 and $14.9 billion after that, against $5.5 billion of cash at the end of the second quarter. Analysts surveyed by FactSet expect negative free cash flow of $10.1 billion in the third quarter, the worst since it began reporting. Baird's Rob Oliver estimates it needs roughly $30 billion in 2027.

Credit desk sources told CNBC the high-yield market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks, because of political pushback against data centers. One source said bond investors want permitting and regulatory questions "substantially resolved" before lending. Janus Henderson's Seth Meyer said pausing "makes sense." In other words, the money is waiting for a politician to say where the power plants may go.

CEO Mike Intrator sent employees a memo saying the company's financing mixes infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity and customer prepayments. He added that it has flexibility to raise equity over time. Translation: if borrowing gets too expensive, it can sell more shares, which existing shareholders tend to find less comforting than the CEO does.

Nvidia's own position is awkward. It invested $2 billion in January at $87.20 a share, and the stock now trades at $61.82. Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave does not need a backstop, and on Thursday told CNBC neocloud demand is "off the charts" but that "there's a scarcity of capital." That is a coherent view: customers are lining up, the money is not. It is also the view of a man who sells the chips those customers rent.

Not everyone is gloomy. Goldman Sachs upgraded CoreWeave to buy, with JPMorgan and Barclays also issuing bullish notes, pointing to its GPU-backed loans and investment-grade customers such as Microsoft and Meta. Goldman wrote that not all neoclouds are created equal. The market, for now, is treating them as if they are.

The next test is CoreWeave's third-quarter report next month, where investors will look for a financing plan. Oliver notes the capital is not needed until the first quarter, which gives management a few months to find buyers for its debt. The midterms, conveniently, arrive first.
articles.wire_headline: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike and stock sinks

articles.headline: Chip Stocks Slide as Investors Remember Memory Can Be Oversupplied, Briefly Forget Again
articles.dek: Tesla's lower spending target and Lam Research's weak forecast hit chipmakers on Thursday, while Nvidia's Jensen Huang said he sees no memory glut by 2029.
articles.catch_up: Memory stocks have fallen for a week after a South Korean opinion column warned the AI boom could slow and flood the market with supply by 2029. On Thursday, MarketWatch said Tesla's spending cut and Lam Research's guidance added to the pressure.
articles.why_it_matters: Memory chips are a core part of AI hardware, so falling prices would squeeze the profits of Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix. Anyone with an index fund is exposed to how long this AI trade keeps its nerve.
body: Chip stocks fell Thursday, with MarketWatch pointing to two causes: Tesla's cut to its near-term spending target and a weaker-than-expected forecast from Lam Research. Lam makes chipmaking equipment, so when it guides low, investors infer that its customers are planning to buy fewer machines. Translation: the shovel seller says fewer people are digging, and the market took note.

CNBC reported that memory stocks had already been battered over the past week. The trigger was an Oct. 15 opinion column in a prominent South Korean publication urging the government to brace for a slowdown in the AI boom. It cited two experts who expected a 'flood of new supply' that would turn memory into 'a red ocean' by 2029, per CNBC's translation.

Translation: a glut means too many chips chasing too few buyers, which pushes prices down and squeezes profit margins at SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron. Elon Musk added to the mood by saying China 'will be making a LOT of RAM in 2028.' The selloff was also fed by China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, announcing a new design architecture that could make it more efficient and let it take share from the incumbents.

Nvidia's Jensen Huang, whose chips depend on memory, offered a different view in a CNBC interview at GTC Berlin. 'You can always use more of it,' he said, which is the sort of forecast one expects from a company that buys the memory. He said HBM, a high-performance type of RAM, will be used for years, and that Nvidia is putting phone-style LPDDR memory into data centers.

Huang also said Chinese manufacturing deserves to be taken very seriously, and that US regulation had 'definitely accelerated' China's chip ambitions. That is a notable admission about export controls, which restrict Beijing's access to top Nvidia chips. CNBC noted that some Chinese firms still reach that computing power through data centers in Southeast Asia.

The wider market showed the same unease. CNBC's Investing Club recap said another wave of selling hit the AI trade, with Huang's remark about a 'scarcity of capital' for neoclouds like CoreWeave, Meta's AI funding comments and Lam's guidance all possibly contributing. GE Vernova, whose gas turbines power the AI buildout, fell almost 10% a day after rising on bullish comments from SpaceX. As one portfolio director put it, the market has 'no memory from one day to the next,' which is an unusual flaw in a memory-focused sell-off.

Money moved into defensive sectors, with healthcare and consumer staples the best performers in the S&P 500. Bond yields fell even as oil rose, which CNBC described as a flight to safety. Meta dropped nearly 6% despite strong revenue growth, with the club suggesting its plan to create a new class of non-voting stock to help fund AI spending might be the overhang.

For context, the 10-year Treasury yielded 5.12% as of Oct. 20, and the S&P 500 tracker SPY closed at 764.95 on Oct. 22. With safe assets paying that much, investors have a fresh reason to ask whether a 2029 chip glut is worth worrying about now. Watch whether Lam's caution spreads to other equipment makers, and whether anyone outside Nvidia's earnings call agrees that memory demand has no ceiling.
articles.wire_headline: Two big reasons Micron and other chip stocks are falling on Thursday

articles.headline: Central Banks Brace to Raise Rates Into Slumping Housing, Frozen Hiring, and Fuel Bills
articles.dek: UK inflation hit 3.5% and US housing data sank, yet markets still expect both central banks to hike, because prices are the problem that currently has a mandate.
articles.catch_up: An oil-supply shock tied to the U.S.-Iran war and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has pushed fuel prices sharply higher, reviving inflation on both sides of the Atlantic. Central banks that had hoped to be cutting rates are now weighing increases.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher policy rates tend to push up mortgage and borrowing costs just as housing is already weak and hiring is soft. Anyone with a variable-rate loan, a house to sell, or a budget to balance should expect no relief soon.
body: UK inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, the Office for National Statistics said Wednesday, above the 3.4% economists polled by Reuters had forecast, according to CNBC. It was the third straight monthly rise, after 2.9% in July and 3.1% in August. The main cause was motor fuel, which rose 29.8% over the year, the sharpest jump since the aftermath of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Translation: Britain imports much of its energy, so when a distant war makes oil hard to move, British drivers receive the invoice. Markets now price a 98% chance that the Bank of England raises rates by 25 basis points (a quarter of a percentage point) to 4% next month, per LSEG data cited by CNBC. Most traders also expect another such hike in December.

The central bank is not only looking at petrol. J.P. Morgan Personal Investing strategist Scott Gardner noted that services inflation has accelerated, raising concern about so-called second-round effects. Translation: that is when higher energy costs leak into wages and prices elsewhere, and a one-time shock becomes a habit.

This lands awkwardly on the Chancellor, John Healey, who unveils his first Autumn Budget next week. Separate data showed national debt exceeded £3 trillion for the first time in September, and the cost of servicing it has risen sharply. Healey promised to maintain fiscal discipline while giving families breathing space, which is a commitment to two things that currently cost money in opposite directions. The Institute of Chartered Accountants' Suren Thiru called the Budget a perilous high-wire act.

In the United States, the Federal Reserve faces its own version of the problem. CNBC reported that pending home sales fell 7.3% in September to the lowest level in records going back to 2001, against a forecast drop of 0.4%. Housing starts fell 5.2% versus an expected 0.4% decline, and single-family permits, at 845,000, were the lowest since 2023. Mortgage rates ended September near 7.6%, according to Mortgage News Daily, against about 3% five years ago.

Normally, a housing slump would encourage a central bank to cut rates. But wholesale goods prices rose 2.6%, the fastest pace in a data series going back to 2009, and the latest official CPI reading stands at 3.74%. Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker pointed to the lock-in effect: more than 95% of mortgage borrowers hold a rate below the current market, so they stay put. Translation: homeowners will not trade a cheap loan for an expensive one, so no one sells, and no one can buy what no one sells.

The labor market offers little counterweight. Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000, near the lowest since 1969, yet payrolls grew only 29,000 in September. Employers are neither hiring nor firing, a state economists call low-hire, low-fire and workers call staying exactly where they are. Markets expect the Fed to hold steady next week, with a quarter-point hike likely in December and another in March 2027, per CME's FedWatch tool.

One hopeful note came from NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun, who suggested mortgage rates may be topping out, since they have already risen more than the Fed's own moves. If so, buyers and sellers may emerge from hiding. Until then, the central banks will keep fighting inflation, and housing will keep serving as the collateral damage.
articles.wire_headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% — cementing rate hike expectations

articles.headline: American Airlines Posts Record Revenue, Still Expects to Lose Money, Blames Jet Fuel
articles.dek: The carrier widened its 2026 loss forecast to as much as $1.60 a share and will slow growth next year, as fuel costs swallowed the best sales in its history.
articles.catch_up: Jet fuel prices have jumped since the start of the Iran war, and airlines have been cutting profit forecasts all month. American is the fourth major U.S. carrier to do so, after Delta, United and Southwest.
articles.why_it_matters: Fuel is the largest airline expense after labor, and airfares are already up more than 20% from last year, according to airline reports and federal data. Slower capacity growth at American could mean fewer new seats and fewer new routes, and so less downward pressure on fares.
body: American Airlines said Thursday that it now expects an adjusted 2026 loss of between $1 and $1.60 a share, CNBC reported. In July, its range ran from a loss of 65 cents to a profit of 65 cents. Translation: the best case in the old forecast was a profit, and the best case in the new one is a smaller loss.

The cause is jet fuel. American's fuel bill rose 67.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, to $4.64 billion. Fuel is the biggest cost for an airline after labor, so a spike of that size is less a line item than a change of business model, from selling flights to subsidizing them.

The odd part is that sales were excellent. Third-quarter revenue rose 19.3% to $16.34 billion, above the $16.22 billion analysts expected, according to LSEG estimates cited by CNBC. CEO Robert Isom called it the strongest year-over-year revenue growth of his career. The adjusted loss was 28 cents a share, better than the 35 cents expected, which in earnings season counts as good news. The net loss was $269 million, up from $114 million a year earlier.

Ordinary travelers have been funding some of this. Airfare is up more than 20% from last year, and the company still lost money, which suggests the fuel increase has outrun even the price increases. Delta, United and Southwest all cut their outlooks this month, so American has company, though not the kind it wanted. Delta and United have been profitable rivals, and American has trailed them considerably.

The company's response is to slow capacity growth next year. For the fourth quarter, it forecasts a loss of 50 cents to $1.10 a share, with revenue up as much as 22.5% and capacity up 5.5% to 6.5%. Translation: capacity means seats flown, and growing it more slowly means fewer new seats chasing the same expensive fuel.

Isom said he has great confidence in a return to profitability in 2027. That rests partly on premium travel, which executives said remains strong, and on strategy: new lounges, cabins with more premium seats, seat-back screens returning to narrow-body jets, and a deeper tie-up with Alaska Airlines in trans-Atlantic and trans-Pacific joint businesses. The airline has also named a new network chief this month, part of a management shake-up. It is also close to ordering wide-body planes, and CFO Devon May said the Boeing 787 and the Airbus A330 and A350 are under consideration.
Market data shows why the confidence is a bet rather than a plan. Brent crude was at $115.22 as of Oct. 20. Whether 2027 is profitable depends less on lounges than on where that number goes.
articles.wire_headline: American Airlines forecasts bigger loss in 2026 on fuel spike, plans to slow growth next year
